units.t: Deep Time and the First People
nar: Stone tools and a butchered rhinoceros in Kalinga date human activity in Luzon to roughly 700,000 years ago. Not our species. Homo luzonensis, a small archaic human, was identified from bones in Callao Cave, about 67,000 years old. Modern humans appear in the Tabon Caves of Palawan around 47,000 years ago.

The bigger story is the Austronesian expansion, beginning around 2200 BCE. People sailing outrigger canoes from Taiwan moved south through the Philippines, then spread across an ocean stretching from Madagascar to Easter Island to Hawaii. Filipinos are not an isolated island people. They are part of the largest maritime migration on Earth before European sail.
The Manunggul Jar, from Palawan, is a burial jar about 2,800 years old. On its lid, two figures paddle a boat. A soul being ferried to the afterlife. It is printed on the thousand-peso bill.
American textbooks start Philippine history in 1521. That is like starting American history at Plymouth Rock and calling it complete.
kid: Our family comes from islands. The first people who lived there got in boats they built themselves and sailed there long before anyone had maps. They were some of the best sailors in the world.

quiz.q: How did the first people reach the Philippines?
quiz.why: Austronesian voyagers sailed outrigger canoes south from Taiwan starting around 2200 BCE.

quiz.q: What is the Manunggul Jar?
o: A burial jar showing a soul in a boat
quiz.why: Two figures paddle a boat on its lid — death imagined as a sea voyage. It's on the 1000-peso bill.

quiz.q: Which language is NOT related to Tagalog?
quiz.why: Hawaiian, Malagasy and Maori are all Austronesian — cousins of Tagalog.

quiz.q: Roughly how many islands make up the Philippines?
quiz.why: 7,641. Only about 2,000 are inhabited.

cards.b: The migration from ~2200 BCE that carried seafarers from Taiwan through the Philippines and across the Pacific and Indian Oceans — Madagascar to Hawaii to Easter Island.
Burial jar from Palawan, c. 800 BCE. Two figures paddle a boat on the lid. On the 1000-peso bill.
A small archaic human species found in Callao Cave, Cagayan, dated ~67,000 years ago.

nar: The basic unit of society was the barangay. The word comes from balangay, the plank-built boat that carried a founding group to a settlement. It is still the name for the smallest unit of government in the Philippines today. Real balangay boats, dated to about 320 of the common era, were excavated at Butuan in Agusan del Norte.

Society ran in three tiers. The datu, the chief, and his ruling class. The timawa, the freemen. And the alipin, usually translated as slave, though the reality was closer to bonded debt. Spanish chroniclers flattened all of this into European feudal categories.

Here is what matters most. There was no single kingdom. There were hundreds of independent barangays. Some were thirty households, some were thousands. This is why Spain could conquer the islands with a few hundred men. There was no center to decapitate. But there was also no unified defense.
kid: Barangay means two things at once. A boat, and a neighborhood. The first neighborhoods were just everybody who arrived in the same boat. Who would be in our family's boat?

quiz.q: Where does 'barangay' come from?
quiz.why: Settlements were named for the boats that brought people there. Still the smallest unit of Philippine government.

quiz.q: Who was the datu?
quiz.why: The datu led the barangay and headed its ruling class.

quiz.q: Why could a few hundred Spaniards conquer millions?
o: No unified kingdom existed to defend the islands
quiz.why: Hundreds of independent barangays meant no central defense — and Spain co-opted datus one at a time.

quiz.q: Where were 320 CE balangay boats found?
quiz.why: Butuan, Agusan del Norte, in Mindanao.

cards.b: The basic pre-colonial community, named for the balangay boat. Still the smallest administrative unit today.
Chief of a barangay. Spain kept datus on as cabezas de barangay to collect tribute — how a few hundred Spaniards ruled millions.
Datu (chief and ruling class) → timawa (freemen) → alipin (bonded, often mistranslated as 'slave').
Hundreds of independent barangays. No central kingdom to defend the islands, and no center Spain had to defeat.

units.t: Writing, Gold, and the Trade World
nar: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription, dated to the year 900, is the oldest known written document from the Philippines. It is a debt clearance. A legal receipt. It is written in Old Malay with Sanskrit and Old Javanese vocabulary, and it names Tundun, which is Tondo, in modern Manila.
Two things follow. Literacy and formal legal instruments existed here in the year 900. And the islands were plugged into the trade world of Southeast Asia.
Baybayin was the pre-Hispanic script, a syllabic writing system used across Luzon and the Visayas. Spanish friars learned it and printed with it before it faded under the Roman alphabet.

The archaeology is full of Chinese porcelain from the Song and Ming dynasties. And the goldwork is extraordinary. The Surigao Treasure. Gold sashes, death masks, ceremonial vessels. Almost none of it is known outside the country.
This was not an isolated backwater waiting to be discovered. It was a literate, gold-working, long-distance trading society.
kid: A long time ago Filipinos had their own alphabet. It was called baybayin, and it looked like little curved shapes. Let's write your name in it.

quiz.q: What is the Laguna Copperplate Inscription?
o: A debt clearance — a legal receipt
quiz.why: Dated 900 CE. A mundane legal document, which is exactly why it proves so much.

quiz.q: What was baybayin?
quiz.why: A syllabic script used across Luzon and the Visayas before the Roman alphabet replaced it.

quiz.q: The Copperplate is dated to what year?
quiz.why: 900 CE — the oldest known written document from the Philippines.

quiz.q: Which place in the Copperplate still exists in Manila?
quiz.why: 'Tundun' is Tondo — where Bonifacio would be born a thousand years later.

cards.b: 900 CE. Oldest known Philippine document — a debt clearance in Old Malay with Sanskrit and Old Javanese words. Names Tondo.
Pre-Hispanic syllabic script of Luzon and the Visayas, displaced by the Roman alphabet.
A hoard of pre-colonial goldwork — sashes, vessels, ornaments — showing the wealth of the islands before Spain.
A routine legal document means literacy, law and commerce were already normal in 900 CE.

nar: Islam arrived through trade and missionary work roughly 140 years before Christianity. Karim al-Makhdum reached Sulu around 1380. The Sultanate of Sulu was founded around 1405, the Sultanate of Maguindanao in the early 1500s.
By 1500 Islam had reached Manila. Rajah Sulayman and Rajah Matanda, the rulers Spain fought for the city in 1571, were Muslim.

This matters for everything that follows. Spain never fully conquered Muslim Mindanao and Sulu. The Moro Wars ran for over three hundred years. When the United States took over in 1898, it inherited that war and fought its own version into 1913. The armed conflict in Mindanao today is a direct continuation.

So when Filipinos say the country was colonized for 333 years, that is not true of the whole archipelago. Moro Filipinos will tell you so. It is one of the sharpest fault lines in how the country tells its own story.
kid: The Philippines has always had people who believe different things living on different islands. In the south, people have been Muslim for over six hundred years. Let's find Mindanao and Sulu on the map.

quiz.q: Which arrived in the Philippines first?
quiz.why: Islam reached Sulu around 1380 — about 140 years before Magellan.

quiz.q: Were the rulers of Manila in 1571 Muslim?
quiz.why: Islam had reached Manila by 1500. Spain took a Muslim city.

quiz.q: How long did the Moro Wars last?
quiz.why: Spain never fully conquered the Muslim south. The US inherited the war and fought into 1913.

quiz.q: Why is '333 years of colonization' contested?
o: It isn't true of Muslim Mindanao and Sulu
quiz.why: The slogan describes the Christianized north.

cards.b: c. 1380 in Sulu, roughly 140 years before Christianity.
Founded c. 1405. One of the polities Spain never fully conquered.
Over 300 years of Spanish conflict with the Muslim south, inherited by the US in 1898 and continuing in Mindanao today.
The slogan describes the Christianized north. It erases the south, which was never fully subjugated.

nar: Magellan reached the islands in March 1521, on the Spanish expedition seeking a western route to the Spice Islands. He befriended Rajah Humabon of Cebu, baptized him, and gave his wife the Santo Niño statue that still draws millions to the Sinulog festival.
Then he tried to force the neighboring island of Mactan to submit.
On April 27, 1521, Lapulapu's men killed Magellan in the surf at Mactan. Antonio Pigafetta, the expedition's chronicler, wrote the account, and it is why we know any of it.

Lapulapu is the first national hero of the Philippines on the strength of one battle. But read what happened. He was a datu defending his own island from a foreign force. He was not a Filipino defending the Philippines, because the Philippines did not exist as an idea yet.
Ruy López de Villalobos named the islands Las Islas Filipinas in 1543, after Prince Philip. The country is named for a Spanish king who never set foot on it.
kid: A famous explorer named Magellan sailed all the way around the world. But when he reached a tiny island called Mactan, a chief named Lapulapu stopped him. There are statues of Lapulapu all over the Philippines.

quiz.q: Who killed Magellan?
quiz.why: April 27, 1521, in the surf at Mactan.

quiz.q: Where does the name 'Philippines' come from?
quiz.why: Villalobos named them in 1543. Philip never visited.

quiz.q: What did Magellan give Rajah Humabon's wife?
quiz.why: Still venerated in Cebu, and the center of the Sinulog festival.

quiz.q: What complicates calling Lapulapu a 'national' hero?
o: There was no nation yet — he defended his island
quiz.why: The idea of 'the Philippines' didn't exist for another 350 years.

cards.b: Battle of Mactan. Lapulapu's men kill Magellan.
Datu of Mactan who defeated Magellan. Honored as the first Filipino hero — though he defended an island, not a nation.
Statue Magellan gave Rajah Humabon's wife in 1521. Center of Cebu's Sinulog festival.
Named by Villalobos in 1543 after Prince Philip of Spain, who never set foot there.

nar: The real colonization began in 1565, when Miguel López de Legazpi landed at Cebu with roughly 500 men. In 1571 he took Manila from Rajah Sulayman and made it the capital — a superb natural harbor at the mouth of the Pasig.

Spain's method was cheap and effective. Co-opt the datus. Chiefs who submitted kept their status as cabezas de barangay and principalía, collected tribute for Spain, and were exempted from forced labor. The colonial state was remarkably thin. At times only a few hundred Spaniards were in the entire archipelago, because the whole thing ran on Filipino intermediaries.
Intramuros, the walled city, went up through the 1570s to 1590s. Stone walls, a fort, churches, and a Spanish city inside them, with everyone else outside.

Think about what three centuries of that does. It is not just that Spain ruled. Spain ruled through a Filipino elite whose power depended on the arrangement. That structure does not vanish when the colonizer leaves.
kid: Spain sent people to live in the islands, and they made Manila their main city because it had a really good harbor for ships. Let's find Manila Bay on the map.

quiz.q: Who began the actual Spanish colonization?
quiz.why: Legazpi landed at Cebu in 1565 with about 500 men.

quiz.q: When did Spain take Manila?
quiz.why: 1571, from Rajah Sulayman. It became the colonial capital.

quiz.q: What was Intramuros?
o: The walled Spanish city in Manila
quiz.why: Latin for 'within the walls.' Spanish inside, everyone else outside.

quiz.q: How did Spain rule millions with a few hundred Spaniards?
o: By co-opting datus as local tax collectors
quiz.why: Datus became cabezas de barangay, keeping status in exchange for collecting tribute.

cards.b: Legazpi lands at Cebu. Spanish colonization begins — 44 years after Magellan died.
Legazpi takes Manila from Rajah Sulayman and makes it the capital.
The walled city of Manila. Spanish inside the walls; Filipinos, Chinese and mestizos outside.
The native elite Spain preserved and ruled through. Its descendants dominate Philippine politics to this day.

nar: For 250 years, one or two ships a year sailed Manila to Acapulco and back. Chinese silk, porcelain and spices went east. Mexican silver came west. One of the first global trade circuits in history, and Manila was its hinge.
Three consequences worth sitting with.

First, the Philippines was governed from Mexico, not Madrid, until 1821. Filipino food, language and Catholicism carry a Mexican accent for exactly this reason. Adobo, menudo, kalabasa, sayote, kamatis, tsokolate.

Second, a large Chinese community, the Sangley, grew in Manila's Parián district — and was massacred repeatedly, in 1603, 1639, 1662 and 1686, in the tens of thousands. Chinese-Filipino identity, and the mestizo class that later produced the nationalist movement, comes out of that history.
Third, the islands ran at a loss. The colony was subsidized every year from Mexico. Spain kept it for prestige, position and souls. Not for profit.
kid: For two hundred and fifty years, one big ship a year carried everything between the Philippines and Mexico. That's why a lot of Filipino food has Spanish and Mexican names. Can you name some?

quiz.q: The galleon trade ran between Manila and —
quiz.why: One or two ships a year, for 250 years.

quiz.q: Until 1821 the Philippines was governed from —
quiz.why: A dependency of New Spain, which is why Filipino culture carries a Mexican accent.

quiz.q: Who were the Sangley?
quiz.why: They lived in the Parián and were massacred repeatedly in the 1600s.

quiz.q: Was the colony profitable for Spain?
o: No — it was subsidized from Mexico
quiz.why: Spain kept it for prestige, strategy and conversion, not money.

cards.b: 1565–1815. One or two ships a year, Manila to Acapulco. Chinese goods east, Mexican silver west.
Until 1821 the Philippines was run as a dependency of New Spain — the reason Filipino food and words feel Mexican.
The Chinese community of Manila's Parián. Massacred repeatedly — yet the source of the mestizo class that led the nationalist movement.
Adobo, menudo, kalabasa, sayote, kamatis, mais, tsokolate — much of it via Mexico, not Spain.

nar: This unit explains the texture of Filipino life more than any other.

Reducción was the policy of forcing scattered settlements into towns, bajo la campana — under the bell, within earshot of a church. It physically restructured the country. The plaza, church and municipio layout across the Philippines today is a colonial artifact.
Encomienda granted a Spaniard the right to collect tribute from a population. Polo y servicios was forced labor, forty days a year, on ships, roads and churches.

Because there were so few Spaniards outside Manila, the friar became the effective government of most towns. Priest, tax supervisor, census keeper, school inspector and censor, all one man. That is why the revolution, when it came, aimed at the friars first.

But Filipinos did not simply receive Catholicism. They remade it. The Pasyon, the sung narrative of Christ's suffering, local saints, festivals, folk practice. The historian Reynaldo Ileto argued the Pasyon gave ordinary Filipinos the language for uprising — a story about a poor man who dies and rises against the powerful.
kid: Every town got a church right in the middle, and everyone had to live close enough to hear the church bell. That's why Philippine towns still have a big plaza with a church on it.

quiz.q: What was reducción?
o: Forcing settlements into towns around a church
quiz.why: Bajo la campana — 'under the bell.' It permanently restructured how Filipinos live.

quiz.q: What was polo y servicios?
quiz.why: Men were conscripted for shipbuilding, roads and construction.

quiz.q: In most towns, who was the effective government?
quiz.why: Priest, tax supervisor, census keeper, school inspector and censor — one man.

quiz.q: What is the Pasyon?
o: A sung narrative of Christ's suffering
quiz.why: Ileto argued it gave ordinary Filipinos a language for uprising.

cards.b: Concentrating scattered settlements into towns within earshot of a church bell. It created the modern Philippine town.
Forced labor, 40 days a year, on ships, roads and churches.
With few Spaniards outside Manila, the parish priest was tax supervisor, census keeper, school inspector and censor. Hence the revolution's target.
The sung Passion narrative. Ileto argued it gave ordinary Filipinos the vocabulary of revolution.

nar: There were well over two hundred revolts in 333 years. The story of a docile colony is false. The story of successful early resistance is also false. Both are true at once.
Lakandula and Sulayman rose in 1574, Manila's displaced rulers, timing it with the Chinese pirate Limahong's attack.
Sumuroy rose in Samar in 1649, against forced labor shipping men to the Cavite shipyards.

Dagohoy rose in Bohol in 1744, and that revolt lasted 85 years, until 1829. The longest in Philippine history. It began over a priest refusing his brother a Christian burial, and it outlived Dagohoy himself by decades.

Diego Silang rose in Ilocos in 1762, allied with the British, and was assassinated. His wife Gabriela Silang took command and led until her capture and execution in 1763. She is the country's most prominent woman revolutionary.
They all failed, for the same reasons. Local grievances. Local scope. No shared language of nation. That missing ingredient is what the next century supplies.
kid: A man named Dagohoy went up into the mountains of Bohol and refused to obey the Spanish for eighty-five years. That's longer than most people live. His people kept it going even after he died.

quiz.q: What was the longest revolt in Philippine history?
quiz.why: 1744–1829. It outlived Dagohoy by decades.

quiz.q: Who was Gabriela Silang?
o: A revolutionary who led after her husband was assassinated
quiz.why: She took command in Ilocos in 1763 and was executed the same year.

quiz.q: Roughly how many revolts under Spanish rule?
quiz.why: The 'docile colony' story is false — but so is the story of successful early resistance.

quiz.q: Why did all these revolts fail?
o: Local in grievance and scope, with no shared idea of nation
quiz.why: That missing ingredient is what the 1800s supply.

cards.b: Bohol, 1744–1829. Eighty-five years, the longest in Philippine history. Began over a denied Christian burial.
Took command of Ilocos rebel forces after her husband Diego was assassinated in 1763. Executed the same year.
Every one was local — local grievance, local scope, local language. No shared national idea.
Samar, 1649. Against forced labor sending men to the Cavite shipyards.

units.t: The British Interlude and the Opening of Manila
nar: Two quiet developments that change everything.
First: from 1762 to 1764 the British occupied Manila during the Seven Years War. Two full years. Spain suddenly looked mortal, and Filipinos noticed. Silang's revolt was a direct consequence.
Second: in 1834 Manila was opened to world trade. Then in 1869 the Suez Canal opened, cutting the voyage to Europe from months to weeks. Cash crops boomed — sugar, abaca, tobacco.

A wealthy Chinese-mestizo and Filipino landowning class emerged from that boom. And they did something explosive with the money. They sent their sons to university. First in Manila, then Madrid, Barcelona and Paris.
Those sons are the ilustrados. The enlightened ones. Spain built the class that would end Spanish rule, and it did it by accident, through economics.
kid: When ships started going faster, ideas traveled faster too. Rich Filipino families started sending their sons all the way to Europe for school. Those sons came back with big ideas.

quiz.q: Who occupied Manila from 1762 to 1764?
quiz.why: During the Seven Years' War. It showed Filipinos that Spain could be beaten.

quiz.q: What did the 1869 Suez Canal do?
o: Cut travel to Europe from months to weeks
quiz.why: Faster ships meant faster goods — and faster ideas.

quiz.q: Who were the ilustrados?
o: European-educated sons of the Filipino landowning class
quiz.why: 'The enlightened.' Their education was funded by the cash-crop boom.

quiz.q: What's the irony of Spain's economic modernization?
o: It created the class that would end Spanish rule
quiz.why: Spain built its own opposition by accident.

cards.b: 1762–64, during the Seven Years' War. Two years that proved Spain was not invincible.
Cut the voyage to Europe from months to weeks. Goods and ideas both moved faster.
'The enlightened' — European-educated sons of the new landowning class. The nationalist movement's founders.
Spain's economic opening created the wealthy class that funded the education that produced the revolution.

nar: This is the hinge year. Learn it properly.

Filipino secular priests had been pushing for the right to run their own parishes. The Spanish friar orders refused. In January 1872, about two hundred Filipino soldiers and workers at the Cavite arsenal mutinied over the loss of their tax and labor exemptions. It was small, and it was crushed in days.

Spain used it as a pretext. Three Filipino priests — Mariano Gómez, José Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, remembered together as GomBurZa — were tried on flimsy evidence and publicly garroted at Bagumbayan on February 17, 1872.

The intent was to terrify the reform movement into silence. The effect was the opposite. Executing three priests, in public, not rebels but priests, turned a narrow clerical dispute into a national grievance overnight.
José Rizal was ten years old. He later dedicated El Filibusterismo to those three men. His brother Paciano had been Burgos's student and housemate.
Filipino nationalism has a birth date, and this is the closest thing to it.
kid: Three priests were punished very badly for something they didn't do. It made people all over the country angry at the same time, which had never happened before. That's when Filipinos started thinking of themselves as one people.

quiz.q: What does GomBurZa stand for?
o: Gómez, Burgos, Zamora — three executed priests
quiz.why: Garroted publicly on February 17, 1872.

quiz.q: What was the pretext for their execution?
quiz.why: About 200 arsenal workers mutinied. Spain used it to destroy the reform movement.

quiz.q: How old was Rizal in 1872?
quiz.why: He later dedicated El Filibusterismo to GomBurZa.

quiz.q: What did Spain intend, and what happened?
o: Intended to silence the movement; instead created a national grievance
quiz.why: Public executions of priests turned a clerical dispute into a nationwide cause.

cards.b: GomBurZa publicly garroted at Bagumbayan. The birth date of Filipino nationalism.
January 1872. About 200 arsenal workers mutinied over lost exemptions. Crushed in days, then used as a pretext.
Filipino secular priests demanded the right to run parishes; Spanish friar orders refused. The grievance behind 1872.
The Manila execution ground where GomBurZa died in 1872 and Rizal in 1896. Today it's Rizal Park.

nar: The ilustrados in Europe organized. Their goal was not independence. It was reform. Representation in the Spanish Cortes. Equal legal status. Secularization of the parishes. Freedom of speech and assembly.

The key figures: Marcelo H. del Pilar, the sharpest polemicist and editor of La Solidaridad. Graciano López Jaena, the orator. And José Rizal, the novelist. La Solidaridad was published in Barcelona and Madrid from 1889.
They failed completely. Spain conceded nothing. Del Pilar died penniless of tuberculosis in Barcelona in 1896.

But they created something that outlasted them. For the first time, people from Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao, speaking entirely different languages, wrote about themselves as one people. Filipino. A word that had previously meant Spaniards born in the islands. They took the colonizer's word for himself and claimed it. That is the invention of a nation on paper, before it existed in fact.
kid: Some young Filipino men went far away to school in Europe. They wrote newspapers asking for their country to be treated fairly. Nobody listened, but they were the first people to write about Filipinos as one big family.

quiz.q: What did the Propaganda Movement want?
quiz.why: Not independence. Reform. They asked for 15 years and got nothing.

quiz.q: What was La Solidaridad?
o: The movement's newspaper, published in Spain
quiz.why: Barcelona and Madrid, from 1889, edited by Marcelo H. del Pilar.

quiz.q: Originally, who did 'Filipino' refer to?
quiz.why: The ilustrados seized the colonizer's word for himself. That's a political act.

quiz.q: Was the movement successful at its stated goal?
quiz.why: Total failure at reform. Total success at inventing a national identity.

cards.b: 1880s–1895. European-based ilustrado campaign for reform — not independence.
The movement's newspaper, Barcelona and Madrid, from 1889. Edited by Marcelo H. del Pilar.
Originally meant Spaniards born in the islands. The ilustrados seized it — inventing a nation in language first.
It failed entirely at reform, and succeeded entirely at creating a shared national identity across languages and islands.

nar: Doctor, ophthalmologist, novelist, poet, sculptor, fencer, polyglot. Educated at Ateneo and Santo Tomas, then Madrid, Paris and Heidelberg.

Noli Me Tángere, 1887. A novel about a young man returning from Europe to a town run by friars, and what happens to his hopes. El Filibusterismo, 1891. The darker sequel, the same man returned as a bitter revolutionary. Both banned. Both read anyway.

In 1892 he came home and founded La Liga Filipina, a civic reform group. He was arrested within days and exiled to Dapitan, in Mindanao, for four years, where he practiced medicine, ran a school and built a water system.

The Katipunan launched its revolution in 1896. Rizal, en route to Cuba as a volunteer doctor, was arrested, brought back, tried for rebellion, and shot at Bagumbayan on December 30, 1896. He was thirty-five. The night before, he wrote Mi Último Adiós and hid it inside an oil lamp.

Here is the complication most people skip. Rizal opposed the armed revolution. He said so at his trial and in a written manifesto. The country made a revolutionary martyr out of a man who thought the revolution was premature. And the American colonial government later promoted Rizal as national hero precisely because he was not Bonifacio.
kid: The most famous Filipino who ever lived was a doctor who wrote books. His name was José Rizal. The night before he died he wrote a poem and hid it inside a lamp so his family would find it.

quiz.q: What are Rizal's two novels?
o: Noli Me Tángere and El Filibusterismo
Mi Último Adiós and La Liga
quiz.why: 1887 and 1891. Both banned, both read anyway.

quiz.q: When was Rizal executed?
quiz.why: Rizal Day. Shot at Bagumbayan at age 35.

quiz.q: Did Rizal support the armed revolution?
o: No — he opposed it as premature
quiz.why: He said so at his trial and in a written manifesto. The country made him a martyr anyway.

quiz.q: Why did the Americans promote Rizal as national hero?
o: Because he wasn't Bonifacio — a reformer is safer than a revolutionary
quiz.why: Honoring the man who opposed armed revolt was convenient for a new colonizer.

cards.b: 1887. Rizal's first novel — a young man returns from Europe to a town run by friars.
Rizal executed at Bagumbayan, age 35. Now Rizal Day.
The poem Rizal wrote the night before his execution and hid inside an oil lamp.
Requires every Filipino college student to study Noli and El Fili. No other country mandates two specific novels by law.

nar: The day after Rizal's arrest in July 1892, Andrés Bonifacio founded the Katipunan — Kataastaasang Kagalanggalangang Katipunan ng mga Anak ng Bayan. A secret revolutionary society with initiation rites, blood compacts and codenames.

Bonifacio matters because of who he was. A warehouse clerk from Tondo. Self-educated. Working class. Not an ilustrado, not European-trained, not wealthy. He read Rizal's novels and the French Revolution and turned that into an organization of tradesmen and laborers, tens of thousands strong.

In August 1896 the Spanish discovered it. Bonifacio and his men tore up their cédulas, the residence tax certificates marking them as colonial subjects, in the Cry of Pugad Lawin. The exact site and date are still disputed among historians.
The revolution began. The Katipunan attacked at San Juan del Monte and lost. But the countryside rose anyway. It was no longer one man's revolt. It was a war.
kid: People joined a secret club to make the Philippines free. It had secret handshakes and secret names. When they were ready, they tore up their government papers to show they weren't going to obey anymore.

quiz.q: Who founded the Katipunan?
quiz.why: July 1892, the day after Rizal's arrest.

quiz.q: What did Bonifacio do for a living?
quiz.why: Self-educated, working class. Not an ilustrado — part of why he's remembered differently.

quiz.q: What did the Katipuneros tear up in 1896?
quiz.why: The cédula marked you as a colonial subject. Tearing it was the act of refusal.

quiz.q: What kind of organization was the Katipunan?
o: A secret society with rites and codenames
quiz.why: Secrecy was the point — the open approach had failed.

cards.b: Founded July 1892 by Bonifacio. A secret revolutionary society that grew into the tens of thousands.
Warehouse clerk from Tondo, self-educated, working class. Founded the Katipunan and started the revolution.
The residence tax certificate marking a colonial subject. Tearing them up in August 1896 was the revolution's opening act.
August 1896 — the declaration of revolution. Exact site and date still disputed.

units.t: Tejeros and the Death of Bonifacio
nar: The hard unit. The revolution turned on itself.

Emilio Aguinaldo, a young mayor from Cavite, was winning battles while Bonifacio was losing them. Cavite's revolutionaries split into two factions, and at the Tejeros Convention in March 1897 they voted to replace the Katipunan with a revolutionary government.

Aguinaldo was elected president in absentia. Bonifacio, founder of the entire movement, was elected Director of the Interior. Then a delegate objected that he was not educated enough to hold even that post.

Bonifacio declared the election void and walked out. Aguinaldo's men arrested him. He was tried for sedition and treason before a court of Aguinaldo's own officers. On May 10, 1897, Bonifacio and his brother Procopio were executed in the mountains of Maragondon.
The revolution killed its founder in its first year.
Then it stalled. In December 1897 Aguinaldo signed the Pact of Biak-na-Bato, accepted money, and went into exile in Hong Kong.
kid: This one is sad, so we'll keep it short. The people fighting for freedom started arguing with each other, and it hurt them badly. It's a good reminder that teams have to stay together.

quiz.q: What happened at the Tejeros Convention?
o: Aguinaldo elected president; Bonifacio demoted and insulted
quiz.why: A delegate objected that Bonifacio wasn't educated enough even for Director of the Interior.

quiz.q: How did Bonifacio die?
quiz.why: Tried by a court of Aguinaldo's own officers, then executed with his brother Procopio.

quiz.q: What was the Pact of Biak-na-Bato?
o: A December 1897 deal — Aguinaldo took money and went into exile
quiz.why: The revolution stalled and Aguinaldo went to Hong Kong.

quiz.q: Which man has a national holiday?
quiz.why: Bonifacio Day. Aguinaldo, who lived until 1964, has none.

cards.b: March 1897. Aguinaldo elected president; Bonifacio demoted and publicly insulted.
Bonifacio and his brother Procopio executed at Maragondon by order of a court of Aguinaldo's officers.
Cavite mayor who took over the revolution, ordered Bonifacio's death, declared independence in 1898, and lived until 1964.
The revolution executed its own founder in its first year, and the man who ordered it never faced consequences.

nar: The year to know cold.

April 1898. The United States declares war on Spain over Cuba. May 1st, Commodore Dewey destroys the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay in a single morning. The Americans bring Aguinaldo back from Hong Kong on an American ship. He believed, and maintained until his death, that the Americans had promised independence.

June 12, 1898. Aguinaldo declares independence from the balcony of his house in Kawit, Cavite. The flag is unfurled. The national march is played for the first time. This is Philippine Independence Day.

August 13, 1898. The Mock Battle of Manila. Spain and the United States secretly arrange a staged battle so Spain can surrender to Americans rather than Filipinos. Filipino troops, who had the city under siege, are barred from entering.

December 10, 1898. The Treaty of Paris. Spain cedes the Philippines to the United States for twenty million dollars. No Filipino is present. No Filipino is consulted. A country that declared independence six months earlier is sold, by a nation that no longer controlled it, to a nation that had never held it.
kid: June twelfth is Philippine Independence Day, like the Fourth of July but for the Philippines. Let's draw the flag. The sun has eight rays and there are three stars, and each one means something.

quiz.q: When is Philippine Independence Day?
quiz.why: June 12, 1898 — Aguinaldo's declaration at Kawit, Cavite.

quiz.q: How much did the US pay Spain for the Philippines?
quiz.why: Treaty of Paris, December 10, 1898. No Filipino was present or consulted.

quiz.q: What was the Mock Battle of Manila?
o: A staged battle so Spain could surrender to Americans, not Filipinos
quiz.why: August 13, 1898. Filipino troops besieging the city were barred from entering it.

quiz.q: Why is the Treaty of Paris called a betrayal?
o: A country that had declared independence was sold without being consulted
quiz.why: Spain sold territory it no longer controlled to a nation that had never held it.

cards.b: Aguinaldo declares independence at Kawit, Cavite. Philippine Independence Day.
August 13, 1898. Spain and the US stage a battle so Spain can surrender to Americans. Filipino troops locked out of the city they besieged.
December 10, 1898. Spain cedes the Philippines to the US for 20 million dollars. No Filipino present, none consulted.
Eight sun rays for the first eight provinces to revolt; three stars for Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao. Flown red-side-up in wartime.

nar: The most important unit in this curriculum, and the one you were never taught.

January 23, 1899. The Malolos Republic is inaugurated under a written constitution, with Apolinario Mabini — paralyzed, brilliant, the Sublime Paralytic — as chief strategist. It is the first constitutional republic in Asia.
February 4, 1899. An American sentry shoots a Filipino soldier at the San Juan bridge. The Philippine-American War begins.
It was declared over in 1902. It was not over. Moro resistance in Mindanao and Sulu continued to 1913.

Hold these numbers. Roughly 4,200 American dead. Filipino combatant deaths estimated around 20,000. Civilian deaths from violence, famine and disease commonly estimated at 200,000 or more, some scholarly estimates far higher. The figures are contested. The scale is not.
Balangiga, Samar, 1901. Filipino townspeople killed 48 American soldiers. General Jacob Smith ordered Samar turned into a howling wilderness and ordered the killing of males over ten.
Bud Dajo, 1906. American forces killed roughly 600 to 1,000 Moros, largely non-combatants, trapped in a volcanic crater.
Concentration camps and the water cure — waterboarding — were used, and were the subject of Senate hearings in 1902.
General Antonio Luna, the Filipino army's best commander, was assassinated in 1899 by soldiers loyal to Aguinaldo.
Back in the States this was fiercely contested. The Anti-Imperialist League included Mark Twain and Andrew Carnegie. It lost.
This war killed more Filipino civilians than the entire American Civil War killed soldiers on both sides. Most American high school graduates have never heard of it. That is not an accident.
kid: We'll skip most of this one, it's a war and it's hard. The short version. Right after the Philippines became free, another country decided to take over, and Filipinos had to fight all over again.

quiz.q: What was the Malolos Republic?
o: The first constitutional republic in Asia, January 1899
quiz.why: Inaugurated January 23, 1899, with Apolinario Mabini as chief strategist.

quiz.q: Estimated Filipino civilian deaths in the war?
quiz.why: From violence, famine and disease. More than the US Civil War killed soldiers on both sides.

quiz.q: Who was Apolinario Mabini?
o: The paralyzed strategist of the Malolos Republic
quiz.why: The 'Sublime Paralytic' — intellectual architect of the first Philippine republic.

quiz.q: Which famous American opposed the war?
quiz.why: Twain and Andrew Carnegie were in the Anti-Imperialist League. They lost.

quiz.q: Who assassinated General Antonio Luna in 1899?
quiz.why: The Filipino army's best commander, killed by his own side. See the film Heneral Luna.

cards.b: January 23, 1899. The first constitutional republic in Asia.
The 'Sublime Paralytic' — paralyzed by polio, and the architect of the first Philippine republic.
~4,200 American dead, ~20,000 Filipino combatants, 200,000+ civilians. Contested figures, uncontested scale.
Samar townspeople killed 48 US soldiers. Gen. Jacob Smith ordered Samar made 'a howling wilderness.'
US forces killed roughly 600–1,000 Moros, largely non-combatants, trapped in a volcanic crater in Sulu.

units.t: Colonial Schooling and the Long Goodbye
nar: American colonialism was different in method, not in fact. Its central instrument was education in English.

In 1901 the United States shipped in about 500 American teachers aboard the USS Thomas. The Thomasites. They built a public school system, in English, across the archipelago within a single generation.

This is why the Philippines is one of the largest English-speaking countries in the world. It is why Filipino nurses, seafarers and call centers staff the global economy. And it is why an enormous amount of pre-colonial and Spanish-era knowledge became inaccessible to ordinary Filipinos in one generation. Both halves of that sentence are true.

The political timeline. The Jones Law of 1916 promised eventual independence and created an elected Philippine Senate. The Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934 set a ten-year timetable, and it passed partly because American farm lobbies and nativists wanted Filipino labor excluded, which it accomplished by reclassifying Filipinos as aliens. The Commonwealth was established in 1935 with Manuel L. Quezon as president.
Meanwhile the manong generation, tens of thousands of young Filipino men, went to Hawaii's plantations and California's fields. They met anti-miscegenation laws and the Watsonville riots of 1930.
kid: American teachers came on a big ship and started schools all over the Philippines where everybody learned English. That's why so many Filipinos speak English today.

quiz.q: Who were the Thomasites?
o: About 500 American teachers who arrived in 1901
quiz.why: Named for the ship, the USS Thomas.

quiz.q: Why is the Philippines a major English-speaking country?
quiz.why: The direct root of the modern nursing, seafaring and call-center economies.

quiz.q: Tydings-McDuffie (1934) passed partly because —
o: US farm lobbies and nativists wanted Filipino labor excluded
quiz.why: Independence granted partly for the wrong reasons — it reclassified Filipinos as aliens.

quiz.q: Who were the 'manongs'?
o: Young Filipino men working Hawaii plantations and California fields
quiz.why: They faced anti-miscegenation laws and the 1930 Watsonville riots.

cards.b: ~500 American teachers who arrived in 1901 aboard the USS Thomas and built an English-language school system across the archipelago.
It gave Filipinos access to the global economy — and cut them off from their own pre-colonial and Spanish-era records in one generation.
First president of the Philippine Commonwealth, 1935.
Tens of thousands of young Filipino men in Hawaii's plantations and California's fields, facing anti-miscegenation laws and the 1930 Watsonville riots.

nar: Japan attacked the Philippines on December 8, 1941, hours after Pearl Harbor. MacArthur's air force was destroyed largely on the ground.
April 1942. The Bataan Death March. Roughly 60,000 to 80,000 Filipino and American prisoners force-marched some 65 miles. Thousands died on the road. Corregidor fell in May.

Then three years of occupation, and one of the largest guerrilla resistance movements of the war — including the Hukbalahap, the peasant anti-Japanese army in Central Luzon, which will matter enormously afterward.

October 1944, Leyte Gulf, the largest naval battle in history. February to March 1945, the Battle of Manila. Around one hundred thousand Filipino civilians died in a single month, killed by Japanese massacres and American artillery. Manila was the second most destroyed Allied capital of the war, after Warsaw. Intramuros was essentially erased.
Also this. Thousands of Filipina women were forced into sexual slavery by the Japanese military. The surviving lolas campaigned for decades for acknowledgment.

And this. The 1946 Rescission Act, in which the United States Congress stripped Filipino soldiers who fought under American command of the veterans' benefits they had been promised. Partial compensation did not come until 2009.
kid: We're going to skip this one for the little ones. If you're asked: there was a very big war, the Philippines was right in the middle of it, and it was very hard for everybody.

quiz.q: When did Japan attack the Philippines?
quiz.why: MacArthur's air force was destroyed largely on the ground.

quiz.q: Most prisoners on the Bataan Death March were —
quiz.why: US textbooks tell it as an American story. The majority of the men were Filipino.

quiz.q: Roughly how many civilians died in the Battle of Manila?
quiz.why: In about a month. Manila was the second most destroyed Allied capital after Warsaw.

quiz.q: What did the 1946 Rescission Act do?
o: Stripped Filipino veterans of promised US benefits
quiz.why: Partial compensation didn't come until 2009.

cards.b: Japan attacks the Philippines, hours after Pearl Harbor.
April 1942. 60,000–80,000 Filipino and American prisoners marched ~65 miles. Most of them were Filipino.
~100,000 civilians killed in a month. Intramuros erased. Second most destroyed Allied capital after Warsaw.
Congress stripped Filipino soldiers who fought under American command of promised benefits. Partial compensation came in 2009.

nar: No new unit this week. Use it for whatever got skipped, or just take the week with your family.
One note. December thirtieth is Rizal Day. If you want a five-minute lesson over lunch, go back to unit thirteen and read Mi Último Adiós out loud. That is enough.
kid: No lesson this week. It's a holiday.

nar: July 4, 1946. The United States granted independence. Note the date. The Philippines was given the American independence day.

In 1962, President Diosdado Macapagal moved Independence Day to June 12, back to Aguinaldo's 1898 declaration. That is a real act of historical reclamation, and it is why the date is different from what your grandparents may have learned.

Independence came with strings. The Bell Trade Act of 1946 required a constitutional amendment giving Americans parity rights — equal access to Philippine natural resources — as a condition of war reconstruction aid. The 1947 Military Bases Agreement gave the United States 99-year leases on Clark, Subic and other installations.

The Hukbalahap rebellion, the wartime guerrillas now fighting their own government over land tenancy, was the defining internal conflict. Ramon Magsaysay put it down through military pressure and land reform promises, with heavy CIA involvement under Edward Lansdale. He died in a plane crash in 1957.
kid: The Philippines became its own country again in 1946. Later they changed Independence Day to June twelfth, so it would match the very first time Filipinos declared themselves free.

quiz.q: The US granted independence on what date?
quiz.why: The American independence day. Macapagal moved the Philippine holiday to June 12 in 1962.

quiz.q: Who moved Independence Day to June 12?
quiz.why: Returning to Aguinaldo's 1898 declaration.

quiz.q: What did the Bell Trade Act require?
o: A constitutional amendment giving Americans parity rights to Philippine resources
quiz.why: A condition of receiving war reconstruction aid.

quiz.q: What was the Huk rebellion about?
quiz.why: The wartime anti-Japanese guerrillas turned on their own government over peasant land rights.

cards.b: US grants Philippine independence — on the American independence day.
In 1962 Macapagal moved Independence Day to June 12, back to Aguinaldo's 1898 declaration.
Required a constitutional amendment giving Americans equal access to Philippine natural resources in exchange for reconstruction aid.
The wartime anti-Japanese guerrillas fighting the postwar government over land tenancy.

nar: Ferdinand Marcos was elected in 1965 and re-elected in 1969, the first Philippine president to win a second term. Constitutionally, he had to leave office in 1973.

On September 21, 1972, he signed Proclamation 1081 and declared martial law, citing communist and Muslim insurgency. Congress closed. Newspapers closed. Opposition figures were arrested, including Benigno Ninoy Aquino Junior.
Amnesty International and the Philippine government's own Human Rights Victims Claims Board documented the scale. Roughly 70,000 imprisoned. 34,000 tortured. Over 3,200 killed.

Meanwhile foreign debt went from around two billion dollars to over twenty-six billion. Monopolies in sugar and coconut were handed to cronies. Estimates of what the family took run from five to ten billion dollars, and courts in Hawaii, the Philippines and Switzerland have found against the estate.
Ninoy Aquino, released to the United States for heart surgery, flew home and was assassinated on the tarmac at Manila International Airport on August 21, 1983. The airport is named after him now.
This is the most actively contested period in Philippine history right now. It is a live political fight, not a settled question.
kid: Not this one. Save it for when they're older.

quiz.q: When was martial law declared?
quiz.why: Proclamation 1081. Congress closed, newspapers closed, opposition arrested.

quiz.q: Why did Marcos declare martial law in 1972?
o: He was constitutionally required to leave office in 1973
quiz.why: The stated reason was insurgency. The structural reason was term limits.

quiz.q: Roughly how many were tortured under martial law?
quiz.why: ~70,000 jailed, ~34,000 tortured, 3,200+ killed, per Amnesty and the Philippines' own claims board.

quiz.q: What happened on August 21, 1983?
o: Ninoy Aquino assassinated on the airport tarmac
quiz.why: Manila International Airport is named after him now.

cards.b: Marcos signs Proclamation 1081, declaring martial law. Congress and newspapers closed.
~70,000 imprisoned, ~34,000 tortured, 3,200+ killed — per Amnesty International and the Philippines' own claims board.
Ninoy Aquino assassinated on the tarmac at Manila International Airport, now named for him.
The martial law record is the most actively contested subject in Philippine history today — a live political fight, not a settled question.

nar: Marcos called a snap election in February 1986 against Corazon Aquino, Ninoy's widow. The count was blatantly rigged. The government's own tabulators walked out on live television.

February 22nd to 25th, 1986. Defense Minister Enrile and General Ramos defected. Cardinal Sin called people into the streets over Radio Veritas. Hundreds of thousands of unarmed civilians filled Epifanio de los Santos Avenue and blocked tanks with their bodies, with rosaries, and with food. The soldiers would not fire. Marcos flew to Hawaii on February 25th.
People Power became a global template. It is cited as an influence on 1989 in Eastern Europe.

What followed was harder. Cory Aquino survived multiple coup attempts. Mount Pinatubo erupted in June 1991, the second largest eruption of the twentieth century, burying Clark Air Base. And in September 1991 the Philippine Senate voted twelve to eleven to reject renewal of the United States bases treaty. A remarkable act of sovereignty. The Americans left Subic in 1992.
Fidel Ramos grew the economy, then the 1997 Asian financial crisis hit. Joseph Estrada was elected in 1998 and removed in EDSA Two in January 2001.
kid: A whole country walked out into the street and stood in front of army tanks with no weapons at all, just rosaries and food. The soldiers wouldn't shoot them, and the president had to leave the country.

quiz.q: What was EDSA People Power?
o: Hundreds of thousands of unarmed civilians blocking tanks, February 1986
quiz.why: February 22–25, 1986. The soldiers would not fire, and Marcos flew to Hawaii.

quiz.q: Who ran against Marcos in the 1986 snap election?
quiz.why: The count was blatantly rigged and the government's own tabulators walked out on live TV.

quiz.q: What did the Philippine Senate do in September 1991?
o: Voted 12–11 to reject renewal of the US bases treaty
quiz.why: A remarkable act of sovereignty. The Americans left Subic in 1992.

quiz.q: What buried Clark Air Base in 1991?
quiz.why: The second largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century.

cards.b: February 22–25, 1986. Hundreds of thousands of unarmed civilians blocked tanks. Marcos flew to Hawaii.
Ninoy's widow, ran against Marcos in the rigged 1986 snap election and became president after EDSA.
The Philippine Senate votes 12–11 to reject the US bases treaty. The Americans leave Subic in 1992.
Erupted June 1991 — the second largest eruption of the 20th century. It buried Clark Air Base.

nar: Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, 2001 to 2010. Growth alongside the Hello Garci election scandal.

Benigno Aquino the Third, 2010 to 2016. Strong growth, and the case that mattered most abroad: in 2016 an arbitral tribunal under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled overwhelmingly in the Philippines' favor against China's Nine-Dash Line claim in the West Philippine Sea. China rejected the ruling. It remains the legal foundation of the Philippine position.

Rodrigo Duterte, 2016 to 2022. The war on drugs. Police reported around six thousand deaths. Human rights groups and the United Nations estimate twenty to thirty thousand including vigilante killings. The International Criminal Court opened an investigation.
Ferdinand Bongbong Marcos Junior won the 2022 election in a landslide, thirty-six years after his family was driven out.

But structural facts define modern Philippine life more than any president. Around ten percent of Filipinos work abroad, and remittances are roughly eight to nine percent of GDP. That is the biggest fact about the contemporary Philippines, and it is the fact that includes your family. Call centers are a top-tier industry, built directly on the English education from unit eighteen. In Mindanao, the Bangsamoro Organic Law of 2018 created an autonomous region — the current chapter of the conflict that started in unit four.
kid: Lots of Filipino families have somebody working in another country who sends money home to help. That's a very normal Filipino story, and it's our story too.

quiz.q: What did the 2016 arbitral tribunal rule?
o: Overwhelmingly for the Philippines against China's Nine-Dash Line
quiz.why: China rejected the ruling, but it remains the legal foundation of the Philippine position.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of Filipinos work abroad?
quiz.why: Remittances are roughly 8–9% of GDP — the single biggest fact about the modern Philippines.

quiz.q: The call center industry is built on what legacy?
quiz.why: A direct line from the Thomasites in 1901 to the outsourcing economy today.

quiz.q: Estimated drug war deaths per rights groups?
quiz.why: Police reported ~6,000; rights groups and the UN estimate 20,000–30,000.

cards.b: Around 10% of Filipinos work abroad. Remittances are roughly 8–9% of GDP — the defining fact of modern Philippine life.
A UNCLOS tribunal ruled for the Philippines against China's Nine-Dash Line in the West Philippine Sea. China rejected it.
Call centers and outsourcing — built directly on the American colonial English school system.
Created an autonomous region in Muslim Mindanao — the latest chapter of a conflict predating Spain.

nar: The wrap-up, and the one that is actually about your family.

Who chooses the heroes? The American colonial government promoted Rizal over Bonifacio. Marcos put himself on the money. The fight over burying Marcos in the Libingan ng mga Bayani in 2016 was a fight about exactly this.

What is a Filipino? There are around four million Filipino Americans. Filipino American history includes the Delano grape strike. Larry Itliong and the manongs started it in 1965, and Cesar Chavez joined them. American schools teach it as a Mexican American story.

The language question. Filipino is based on Tagalog. There are over 180 languages in the country. Cebuano has more native speakers than Tagalog. A Filipino from Cebu might reasonably ask why the national language is somebody else's.

And balikbayan. There is a specific Tagalog word for someone who returns. Balikbayan. Return to country. A nation with ten percent of its people abroad needed a word for it. Plans to go back are not unusual. They are a national genre.
kid: Where is our family from? Where were you born? Let's put pins on the map — the Philippines, and everywhere our family has lived since.

quiz.q: Who started the Delano grape strike in 1965?
o: Larry Itliong and the Filipino manongs
quiz.why: Chavez joined them. American schools usually teach it as a Mexican-American story.

quiz.q: Which language has more native speakers?
quiz.why: Yet the national language, Filipino, is based on Tagalog. That's a live grievance.

quiz.q: What does 'balikbayan' mean?
o: Someone who returns to the country
quiz.why: Literally 'return to country.' A nation with 10% of its people abroad needed the word.

quiz.q: How many languages are spoken in the Philippines?
quiz.why: Filipino is based on Tagalog — one of them.

cards.b: Filipino labor leader who, with the manongs, started the 1965 Delano grape strike. Chavez joined them — and got the credit.
Tagalog for 'return to country.' A word a nation needs when 10% of its people live abroad.
Filipino is based on Tagalog, but Cebuano has more native speakers and over 180 languages are spoken.
The Americans elevated Rizal over Bonifacio. Marcos put himself on money. The 2016 Libingan burial fight was the same argument.

nar: Whatever you skipped. Or watch Heneral Luna with the older kids and argue about it afterward.
If you want one book to keep going with, Luis Francia's A History of the Philippines, from Indios Bravos to Filipinos. Readable, one volume, the whole arc.
kid: No lesson. Movie week.
